text:
Morgan: Hey team, just got a customer escalaton — they see p99 total latency spike starting around our 2026-03-10 infra change. They say streaming responses are taking much longer total time even though first byte is usually quick. Ticket attached: https://support.example.com/t/51234

Aisha: Can you paste a minimal repro from the customer? streaming vs non-streaming comparisons?

Morgan: Customer provided two curl runs. Streaming (SSE) shows TTFB ~120ms but end-to-end ~4.2s p99. Non-streaming (blocking) for same prompt is ~900ms p99. They suspect chunk coalescing causing long tail.

Carlos: Interesting — opposite of what you'd expect. Any proxy in between? We rolled http2 multiplexing + coalescer last week (http2-mux v2). Could be a handshake/flush heuristic.

Morgan: They are on our hosted API region us-west-2. Path: load-balancer -> edge-proxy -> inference-runtime. They included edge-proxy logs. Searching through them shows repeated entries like:

```
[edge-proxy] 2026-03-11T18:12:05.123Z stream_id=45 queued_for_flush=true queue_depth=3 wait_ms=18 flush_count=1
[edge-proxy] 2026-03-11T18:12:05.240Z stream_id=45 flush_sent bytes=64
[edge-proxy] 2026-03-11T18:12:09.380Z stream_id=45 final_chunk_sent bytes=256 total_time_ms=4260
```
Aisha: That wait_ms=18 heuristic seems small, but why final chunk waits multiple seconds? queue_depth 3 then final chunk after ~4s suggests something else upstream stalled.

Evan: @infra-bot can you surface runtime logs for request id the customer provided? request_id=abc-51234-usw2

infra-bot: runtime logs for request_id=abc-51234-usw2:
```
[runtime] KV_CACHE_HIT=false kernel=gelu_opt seq=1024 token_streaming=true first_token_out=110ms last_token_out=4180ms cpu_ms=12 gpu_ms=62
```
Carlos: Runtime shows tokens streaming out steadily but last_token_out at 4180ms. So runtime did produce last tokens ~4s after first token. Is model quantization or scheduler changed?

Dana: We shipped a small scheduler tweak two days ago that batches low-rate streams to improve throughput. It raises a per-stream flush threshold: min_tokens_before_flush=4 or wait_ms_before_force=2000ms for low-burst streams. That could explain long tail.

Aisha: Okay that lines up. With SSE streaming, small responses might be forced to wait until either token count or time threshold is met; non-streaming aggregates all tokens before returning so it's not hit by that heuristic the same way.

Morgan: Customer's repro shows a short prompt that returns ~18 tokens. If the scheduler waits for groups it could delay final bytes. Their curl (streaming):
```
curl -N -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -H "Accept: text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"prompt":"short prompt","stream":true}' https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate
```
Non-streaming: stream=false returns ~900ms.

Carlos: Repro plan: 1) Run with stream=true and stream=false against same runtime binary; 2) Toggle scheduler flag; 3) Run with HTTP/1.1 (disable http2 multiplexing) to rule out proxy coalescing.

Evan: I kicked off internal repros. Quick findings: 1) Disabling minischeduler (setting min_tokens_before_flush=1) drops streaming p99 to ~700ms. 2) Forcing HTTP/1.1 (no mux) also drops tail in some cases.

Aisha: So both scheduler and http2-mux changes interact. For some small-stream workloads, multiplexer waits to coalesce frames across streams and scheduler waits for tokens — compound delay.

Morgan: Customer wants mitigation ASAP. Recommended steps?

Carlos: Immediate mitigations we can offer customer: 1) As a one-off, they can set header X-Redwood-Stream-Mode: "no-coalesce" (we support this gate) or 2) Use stream=false fallback if they can tolerate extra latency but better p99, or 3) We can create a per-customer runtime override to lower wait_ms_before_force to 50ms for their traffic.

Dana: We should also roll a hotfix: change scheduler default for hosted API to lower wait_ms_before_force for low-token sequences from 2000ms -> 150ms and add guardrails so throughput doesn't regress. But that needs perf regression check.

Aisha: For immediate internal action: open a short-lived rollback of http2-mux coalescing heuristic for us-west-2 only, and apply per-customer override. I'll create a rollout plan.

Morgan: Customer responded: "Thanks — we can try header toggle now." They tried X-Redwood-Stream-Mode:no-coalesce and reported p99 dropped to ~820ms. 

Evan: Good. I'll capture traces and metrics to validate wider impact. We should also add a smoke test for small-token streaming to our perf suite (p95/p99 for 8-32 token responses).

Carlos: Notes for postmortem: root cause is interaction between http2 multiplexing coalescer and new scheduler batching heuristic. Two separate changes compounded for low-token streaming workloads. Mitigations: header escape hatch, per-customer runtime tweak, default scheduler tuning, new perf tests.

Dana: I'll draft change and include perf numbers. Short-term action items:
- Aisha: roll per-customer override + notify customer (in progress)
- Evan: collect traces + dashboards (ETA 2h)
- Carlos: prepare rollback plan for http2-mux coalescer (ETA 3h)
- Morgan: keep customer updated, confirm header test success

Morgan: Customer confirmed stable after header toggle for last hour. They're happy with temp fix but want permanent solution. I'll escalate to account team. :thumbsup:

Evan: Adding follow-ups: add unit test for flush thresholds, add an obs metric for "stream_flush_wait_time" and alert if >500ms p99.

Carlos: Good. Leaving this thread open until rollout or rollback completes. Thanks everyone.
